title: Slack
seoTitle: Design Slack — Team Chat with Channels
description: Design team chat like Slack — workspaces and channels, real-time message delivery over WebSockets, ordered channel history, unread state, search, and very large channels.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is Slack?
blocks.text: Slack is chat for organisations. Each company has a **workspace** with **channels** (public or private) and direct messages. Unlike consumer messengers, history is permanent and searchable, channels can have tens of thousands of members, and people use it from several devices at once all day.

items: Users should be able to send messages to channels and DMs, and receive them in real time.
Users should be able to scroll back through a channel's full history.
Users should see which channels have unread messages and mentions, synced across devices.
Users should be able to search messages in their workspace.
Threads, reactions and file uploads (mentioned briefly).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Messages delivered to online members within ~500 ms.
Messages within a channel are ordered consistently for everyone.
No message loss; history is durable.
Scale to ~1M workspaces, ~20M concurrent connections, and channels with 100k members.
End-to-end encryption (Slack messages are searchable server-side).
**Channel**: workspace, name, type (public, private, DM), members.
**Message**: channel, sender, text, timestamp ID (ordered within the channel).
**Read cursor**: per user per channel, the last message they've read.

blocks.text: 1) Sending and receiving in real time

Clients keep a **WebSocket** to a gateway server. On send, the **Message Service** assigns the message a channel-ordered ID, persists it, and publishes it to the channel's topic. Every gateway that has connected members of that channel is subscribed to the topic and pushes the message to them.

Messages are stored partitioned by **channel ID** and sorted by message timestamp, so "the 50 messages before X" is one range read (Cassandra/Vitess-style sharded MySQL). Clients cache recent history locally and fetch older pages as the user scrolls.

Each user has a **read cursor** per channel. A channel is unread if its latest message ID is greater than the cursor. When the user reads on one device, the cursor update is pushed to their other devices so badges clear everywhere. Mentions are counted separately, as they're more important.

Messages are indexed asynchronously into a search cluster **partitioned by workspace**, so a query only touches that workspace's index and isolation is enforced. Search filters by channels the user can see.
1) How do we fan out to a channel with 100k members?

approach.text: Copy each message into every member's inbox (fan-out on write).

challenges.text: 100k writes per message in a busy announcements channel, mostly for people who aren't online.

approach.text: Store the message once per channel. Look up online members and push to each of their connections.

challenges.text: Looking up and pushing to 100k members from one service is slow and bursty.

approach.text: Each gateway server **subscribes to the channels its connected users belong to**. A message is published once to the channel topic and reaches only the gateways that care (perhaps a few hundred), each of which delivers locally to its connections. Offline members simply see it in history and unread counts when they return. A **channel server** layer can own subscription state per channel to avoid every gateway tracking everything.

challenges.text: Users in thousands of channels mean large subscription sets; gateways subscribe lazily and clients load a "boot" snapshot on connect.

blocks.text: 2) How do we order messages and avoid duplicates?

Each channel's messages get IDs from a single **owner** for that channel (the shard leader or a per-channel sequence), so order is consistent for everyone. Clients send a **clientMsgId**; retries after a timeout are deduplicated, so a flaky connection doesn't post the message twice. Clients show the message optimistically and reconcile when the server's ID arrives.
Mention reconnection: a reconnecting client sends its last seen message ID per active channel and fetches anything newer, so nothing is missed during a disconnect.
3) How do we keep workspaces isolated and scalable?

Shard data by **workspace ID** (with very large enterprises getting dedicated shards), so a workspace's channels, messages and search index live together and queries can't cross tenants. Gateways authenticate each connection to a workspace and only subscribe to that workspace's channels.

quiz.question: Why not copy every message into each member's inbox?
options: Large channels would need 100k writes per message
quiz.explanation: Messages are stored once per channel and delivered to online members.

quiz.question: How does a gateway know which messages to deliver?
options: It subscribes to the channels its connected users belong to
quiz.explanation: Pub/sub per channel limits fan-out to interested gateways.

quiz.question: How is a channel marked unread?
options: A flag per message per user
Its latest message ID is greater than the user's read cursor
quiz.explanation: One cursor per user per channel is cheap and syncs across devices.

quiz.question: What prevents a retried send from posting twice?
options: A client-generated message ID used for deduplication
quiz.explanation: The server ignores repeats of the same clientMsgId.
